If you need a finished photo book by this weekend — a birthday gift, a holiday deadline, or just because — you don't need a design background or a free afternoon to get it done.

Using an AI photo book maker like Pixovo, a simple single-trip or single-event book can be designed in as little as 5 minutes, and most people finish start to finish — including picking size and paper — in under 10.

This guide is the practical walkthrough. If you want the conceptual explanation of how the layout decisions work, that's covered in what an AI photo book maker is. This post skips straight to doing it.

Before you start, you need three things: your phone or a folder of photos on your computer, a stable internet connection to upload them, and a few uninterrupted minutes. This step rarely takes longer than the time it takes your coffee to brew.

Step 1: Choose Your Photos

You have two ways to do this. The manual route means scrolling your camera roll and picking the shots you want yourself, which gives you full control but takes longer the more photos you're choosing from. The faster route is to let the AI select your best shots automatically — based on image quality, faces in focus, and reduced duplicates — then simply remove anything it picked that you'd rather leave out. For a first attempt, letting the AI pick highlights and editing down is almost always faster than starting from a blank selection yourself.

Step 2: Upload to Your Photo Book Maker

Once you've chosen your photos, upload them as a batch rather than one at a time. Most tools, including Pixovo, support drag-and-drop from your phone's camera roll or a folder on your computer. This step takes under a minute regardless of how many photos you're uploading, since it happens in the background while you move on to the next step.

Step 3: Let AI Design the Layout

This is where the AI photo book maker does the bulk of the work — grouping your photos, choosing page layouts, and balancing how much space each photo gets. It happens automatically once your photos finish uploading, and you're shown a complete draft, not a blank canvas, when it's done.

Step 4: Review and Personalize

Now you decide what stays and what changes. You can swap out any photo you don't like, rearrange pages, edit or add captions, and personalize the cover with a title or a name. Nothing here is locked in until you actually place the order, so it's worth spending a minute or two on this step even if the first draft already looks good.

Step 5: Choose Size, Cover, and Paper, Then Order

Last, pick your book's size, cover type, and paper finish for your project — our size guide breaks down which format suits travel books, gifts, and larger keepsake books. Once you confirm your choices, place the order and the printing process begins.

Common Mistakes to Avoid

Even with an AI photo book maker handling the design work, a few habits make the difference between a book you love and one you wish you'd redone:

  • Uploading blurry or very low-resolution photos. A shot that looks fine on a phone screen can look soft once printed at a larger page size.
  • Including too many near-identical shots of the same moment. It dilutes your strongest photos rather than showcasing them.
  • Skipping the cover design because it feels like an afterthought. It's the first thing anyone sees before they open the book at all.
  • Deciding on a size only at checkout. Since size affects how many photos comfortably fit per page, picking it early avoids re-reviewing layouts you've already approved.

An AI photo book vs traditional photo book comes down to one thing: who does the design work. A traditional photo book puts every layout decision on you — pick a template, place each photo, repeat for every page. An AI photo book, like the ones you build on Pixovo, uploads your photos and lets automatic photo book layout software design the pages for you to review and fine-tune from there, instead of starting from a blank page.

Quick Summary

  • AI photo book: you upload photos, the software designs the layout automatically, then you edit and order.
  • Traditional photo book: you manually place every photo on every page yourself, using photo book design software as a blank canvas.
  • Time difference is the biggest gap. A full book that takes 45+ minutes manually often comes together in minutes with AI-assisted layout.
  • AI wins on speed and ease for large or unsorted photo batches; traditional tools win when you want full manual control over every page.
  • Pixovo is built AI-first — with editing available after the first draft, not a manual-only tool.

What Is an AI Photo Book?

An AI photo book is a printed photo book whose page layout was designed automatically by software, not placed page-by-page by hand. You upload your photos, the AI groups and arranges them across every page at once, and you're left reviewing and adjusting a finished first draft rather than building one from scratch. This is the core mechanism behind Pixovo's AI photo book builder: upload photos, let the AI design a personalized layout automatically, then fine-tune colors, text, or theme before ordering.

What Is a Traditional Photo Book?

A traditional photo book is built using template-based photo book design software, where every layout decision — which photo goes where, how it's cropped, how many photos share a page — is made manually by the person creating it. The software provides the canvas and the tools; you provide every decision. This gives complete creative control, but it also means the work scales directly with how many pages and photos you're working with.

AI Photo Book Benefits

The main AI photo book benefits are speed, accessibility, and consistency:

  • Speed — automatic photo book layout removes the single biggest reason people abandon a photo book project halfway through: the repetitive manual work of placing every photo one at a time.
  • Accessibility — no design experience is needed. The AI makes the first round of layout decisions, so someone who's never used photo book design software before ends up with a professional-looking result.
  • Consistency — the AI balances photos and spacing across every page using the same logic throughout, rather than the layout quality drifting as a person gets tired of manually placing photos halfway through a long book.

title: Photo Book Sizes Explained: Which Size Is Actually Right for Your Photos in 2026
author: Pixovo Team

parts.html:
Most people choose the wrong photo book size the first time. They either pick too small and regret cramming a year of memories into a handful of pages, or they pick too large and end up with a book that's awkward to hold, expensive, and ends up on a shelf gathering dust. The decision feels simple on a website form, but it's actually one of the most important choices you'll make when building a photo book. Size affects not just how many photos fit, but how you'll actually use and display the finished book.

Here's what most size guides miss: they tell you the dimensions in inches but never answer the question that actually matters: "Will I want to look at this book in six months, or will it feel like a chore?" This guide covers that gap.

Quick Summary

  • 8x8 is the most portable and affordable size, best for gifts and personal keepsakes; holds roughly 40-160 photos per book depending on layout.
  • 10x10 is the most popular size, balancing portability with generous space; holds 90-360 photos and costs 50% more than 8x8.
  • 12x12 is the coffee-table statement piece, best for weddings and milestone events; holds 160-640 photos but requires table-top viewing.
  • The wrong size choice usually comes down to underestimating how many photos you have or overestimating how much handling you want to do.
  • AI-powered layout (like Pixovo's) handles size differences better than manual design, since the algorithm automatically adjusts density and emphasis for each size.
  • See the difference yourself. Start with a free preview at Pixovo and upload a few photos to see how each size looks with your images.

Why Size Isn't Just About Inches

When you're building a photo book online, size feels like a purely technical choice. But the truth is that size is a decision about how you want to interact with your memories. An 8x8 book you'll actually pull off the shelf and flip through is infinitely more valuable than a 12x12 that's too large to hold comfortably and stays in the closet.

That's why the best size is the one that matches your real habits, not the one that sounds impressive. Here's the secret most guides won't tell you: people underestimate how many photos they want to include. They think "I have 200 photos from our trip, I'll just pick the best 50." Then they start going through them and realize 50 isn't enough to tell the real story. By then, they've already committed to a smaller size and are stuck with a cramped layout.

Conversely, people overestimate their tolerance for handling weight. A 12x12 book is heavier than you'd expect, and it requires two hands and a flat surface to browse comfortably. If you're the type to flip through photo books while sitting on the couch, the larger size turns into a production instead of a pleasure.

The size that works for you depends on three things: how many photos you actually have, what you plan to do with the book (gift, display, archive, or frequent viewing), and your physical comfort holding and handling it.

The price difference is significant. A 12x12 book costs roughly 2x more than an 8x8, and a 10x10 falls in the middle. That price scales with page count too. If you're printing 40 pages at 8x8, you're looking at one price. The same 40 pages at 12x12 will cost substantially more.

What Size Do Most People Actually Choose?

Based on patterns across photo book makers, the 10x10 is the most popular choice by far. It's the Goldilocks size: not too small, not too large, and it feels substantial enough to justify the cost without being unwieldy to handle. Wedding and family photographers almost always recommend 10x10 as the default for a reason.

The 8x8 is chosen most often by people buying gifts or making their first photo book. It's lower risk (less expensive) and easier to gift.

The 12x12 is chosen specifically for occasions, usually weddings or significant anniversaries, where the budget is already allocated and the book is meant to be a statement piece, not an everyday object.

Common Mistakes When Choosing Size (And How to Avoid Them)

Mistake 1: Choosing the Smallest Size to Save Money

The cost difference between sizes looks dramatic online ($19.99 vs $39.99), but it usually evaporates when you account for the full book. An 8x8 with 20 pages and a 12x12 with 60 pages cost roughly the same per photo. If you're cramming 200 photos into an 8x8, you're not saving money, you're compromising quality. The photos are too small to see, captions are microscopic, and the book feels rushed.

Better approach: Choose based on photos, not budget. If you have 300 photos, a 10x10 or 12x12 makes sense. If you have 60 photos, 8x8 is the right call.

Mistake 2: Overestimating How Much Handling You'll Do

People imagine themselves curling up with a large, beautiful photo book every week. In reality, photo books get pulled out maybe 2-3 times a year, usually to show a guest or during a nostalgic moment. A 12x12 that requires setup on a table might get viewed less often than an 8x8 you can grab off the shelf and flip through in bed.

Better approach: Be honest about your habits. If you view photo books rarely (once or twice a year), size matters less. If you view them regularly, portability matters more than impressiveness.

Mistake 3: Not Accounting for the Actual Number of Photos

Almost everyone underestimates their photo count. They think they have 100 good photos from a trip and choose an 8x8. Then they start sorting and realize they have 400 photos and most of them are actually worth keeping. An 8x8 suddenly feels too small.

Better approach: Count your photos first. Sort them into your actual "yes" pile, then choose a size based on that number, not on an estimate.

An 8x8 gets a denser, more compact layout. A 12x12 gets a more spacious, magazine-style layout. The same photos look good at any size because the layout adapts.

Size and Your Photo Collection Matter More Than You Think

The "right" size isn't a universal answer. It's specific to your photos, your habits, and what you plan to do with the book. But the pattern is clear:

Travel or single-event albums with 50-100 photos? Go 8x8. Family albums covering a year of memories? Go 10x10. Weddings, major milestones, or statement pieces? Go 12x12.

The most common regret isn't "I should have gone bigger," it's "I chose a size without counting my photos first." Do that math upfront, and you'll avoid that regret entirely.

Readers naturally expect a timeline, and breaking it disrupts the story more than any layout choice. Below are wedding photo book ideas by style, plus the mistakes that most often make couples want to redo their album later.

Quick Summary

  • Chronological order (getting ready, ceremony, reception) almost always outperforms grouping by photographer or camera.
  • Three layout styles cover most weddings: classic, minimalist, and photo heavy coffee table style.
  • The #1 mistake: too many near identical posed shots crowding out candid and detail moments.

Why Chronological Order Almost Always Works Best

A wedding day already has a natural structure: getting ready, the ceremony, portraits, reception. A wedding photo book reads best when it follows that same order. Grouping photos by who took them (professional photographer vs. phone photos from guests) breaks that narrative and makes the book feel disjointed, even if every individual photo is great. When in doubt, order by when it happened, not by where the photo came from.

Layout Ideas by Style

Classic

Clean, symmetrical layouts with generous white space around each photo. One to three photos per page lets each image breathe. Works well for formal or traditional weddings.

Minimalist

Even simpler than classic. Often just one full page photo per spread, letting the best shots stand completely on their own with almost no competing text or decoration.

Photo Heavy Coffee Table

Denser layouts with collages, several photos grouped per page, designed to be flipped through casually rather than read start to finish. A good fit for weddings with hundreds of guest photos you want to include without editing down to just the best 40.

Common Mistakes to Avoid

  • Too many near identical posed shots. Five almost the same first dance photos crowd out the candid, in between moments that usually end up mattering more months later.
  • Skipping detail shots entirely (the dress, the rings, the venue decor) in favor of only people photos, which flattens the story of the day.
  • Waiting too long. Photo selection gets harder, not easier, the further you get from the wedding, since the specific moments you remember start blurring together.

Honeymoon Photo Book: A Companion Piece, Not a Replacement

A honeymoon photo book works best as its own separate book rather than tacked onto the end of the wedding album. The wedding day and the honeymoon are different stories. Mixing them dilutes both, and a separate honeymoon book gives trip photos the same chronological treatment a travel photo book benefits from.

parts.html:
Most people's phones now hold thousands of photos — often 2,000, 5,000, sometimes tens of thousands — and the overwhelming majority will never be printed, framed, or even looked at again after the day they were taken.

That's not because those memories matter less. It's because turning a messy camera roll into an actual photo book has always meant hours of manual template work most people never get around to finishing. An AI photo book maker exists to remove that bottleneck entirely: upload your photos, and the AI designs the whole book for you in minutes.

What Is an AI Photo Book Maker, Exactly?

An AI photo book maker is a tool that automatically selects, arranges, and designs the pages of a printed photo book from a batch of your uploaded photos — instead of you manually placing each photo into a template one at a time. You upload your photos, the AI groups them, chooses layouts, balances how much space each photo gets, and produces a ready-to-edit book in minutes rather than hours.

Put another way, a traditional photo book tool hands you a blank template and expects you to do the design work yourself. An AI photo book maker does the design work first and hands you a finished draft to review, tweak, and approve. That's the entire shift this category represents — the AI isn't a feature bolted onto an old workflow, it replaces the single most time-consuming part of that workflow: the layout decisions themselves.

You'll see this same idea described a few different ways depending on the brand — some call it simply an AI photo book, others describe the underlying mechanism as automatic photo book layout — but the core idea is consistent across the category: software makes the first pass at page composition, and you make the final call on what actually gets printed.

Why AI Photo Book Makers Exist

The problem an AI photo book maker solves isn't a lack of interest in printed memories. People consistently say they want more physical prints and fewer memories trapped on a phone. The real problem is the blank page.

Building a photo book manually means choosing which of hundreds of near-identical shots to keep, resizing and cropping each one to fit a template, deciding how many photos belong on a page without it looking cluttered, and then repeating that same set of decisions twenty to forty times for a single book. It's not that any single step is difficult — it's that the process is tedious enough that most people start a photo book project and never finish it, which is exactly why so many camera rolls stay unprinted for years.

That's the specific gap an AI photo book maker is built to close. Instead of staring at a blank page and wondering where to start, you start with a finished layout and work backward from there — editing what you don't like instead of building everything from scratch.

How Does AI Photo Book Creation Work?

Understanding how AI photo book creation works in practice makes the value a lot clearer, because it isn't a single trick — it's three layered passes over your photos.

1

Smart Photo Sorting

The AI first sorts your uploaded photos using signals like date, time, and visual similarity — grouping a weekend trip together, separating a birthday party from an ordinary Tuesday, and flagging near-duplicate shots so you're not shown the same moment five times over. This first pass alone removes most of the manual sorting work.

2

Composition Rules

Next, the AI applies basic composition logic to each photo and page: cropping for the strongest composition, avoiding awkward face-cropping, and deciding whether a photo deserves a full page, a half page, or a smaller spot in a grid based on its visual weight and image quality.

3

Page Balance

Finally, the AI paces the entire book — making sure your strongest, most meaningful shots (a wedding kiss, a first birthday cake, a mountain summit) get more visual space than a blurry parking-lot photo that happened to be sitting on your camera roll, and spreading variety across spreads so no section of the book feels repetitive.

What You Still Control vs. What the AI Decides

The AI makes all of those first-pass decisions automatically, but you still control the final result. You can swap any photo, change a layout, edit captions, adjust the cover design, add your own text, and reorder pages before you order. Think of the AI's output as a strong first draft, not a locked final version you're stuck with.

How Long It Actually Takes

Most people go from upload to a finished, reviewable layout in under 10 minutes — a process that can otherwise take 45 to 90 minutes of manual template work for a single book.

The trade-off here is an honest one. A manual tool gives you total control over every pixel from the first click. An AI photo book maker gives up a small amount of that granular control in exchange for a finished starting point — and lets you add the control back in during editing, if that's what you want.

Is an AI Photo Book Maker Worth It?

For most people, yes — specifically because the realistic alternative to using one usually isn't a perfectly designed manual book. It's no book at all. If the real choice is between an AI-assisted book you actually finish and order, versus a manual project that sits half-done in a browser tab for eight months, the AI photo book maker wins by default almost every time.

The calculation changes if design itself is part of the enjoyment for you — some people genuinely like spending an evening arranging every page by hand, and a manual tool suits that preference better. But if the goal is a finished, high-quality photo book of your actual photos rather than a design hobby, an AI photo book maker gets you there with a fraction of the effort and none of the abandoned-project guilt.

A decorative item sits on a shelf for six months and gets moved to the donation pile. But a photo book is different. A well-made photo book gift becomes a keepsake people actually return to, year after year. The question isn't whether photo book gifts work. It's whether you choose the right one for the person and occasion.

Most photo book gift guides throw every idea at the wall: anniversary albums, baby books, travel journals, graduation albums, you name it. But they miss the real question: which gifts people actually want to receive, and which ones they appreciate in theory but never look at again. This guide covers both the ideas and the strategy behind choosing a gift that lands.

Quick Summary

  • Photo book gifts work because they're personal, tangible, and become heirlooms; recipients display them or return to them regularly.
  • Anniversary photo books (10x10 or 12x12) are the most successful occasion-specific gift; they cost $20 to $50 and feel premium.

Photo books occupy a unique space in gift-giving psychology. They're personal without being creepy. They're tangible without being clutter. And unlike most gifts, they become more valuable over time, not less.

Here's why: a physical object you created specifically for someone says, "I spent time on this. I thought about you." That message compounds. The first time they see the gift, they feel appreciated. The next time they show it to someone else, they feel appreciated again. Years later, when they flip through it, the original gesture feels fresh.

Other gifts don't have that longevity. A tech gadget gets replaced. A decorative item becomes outdated. But a photo book becomes a time capsule. The photos don't change. The sentiment doesn't age. If anything, it deepens.

The catch: this only works if the photo book actually gets used. A small, cramped album with tiny photos that's hard to hold gets shelved. A thoughtfully sized album with good photos and personal touches gets displayed on the coffee table or pulled off the shelf regularly.

Common Mistakes Gift-Givers Make (And How to Avoid Them)

Mistake 1: Choosing 8x8 for a Major Occasion

An 8x8 photo book is perfect for travel or a baby's first year. It's terrible for a wedding or anniversary gift. When recipients open it expecting something substantial and see a small book with tiny photos, they're often disappointed. The gesture feels diminished by the size.

Fix: For weddings, anniversaries, and major milestones, go 10x10 or 12x12. The extra $10 to $20 is worth the impact.

Mistake 2: Just Filling It With Photos, No Context

A photo book with 200 beautiful photos but zero captions or personal notes feels lazy, even if it took hours to create. Recipients wonder "why these photos? what do they mean?" Context makes the difference.

Fix: Add brief captions, dates, locations, or short stories. Or include handwritten notes from friends. Even two words per page transforms a photo dump into a narrative.

Mistake 3: Forgetting to Personalize for Multi-Person Occasions

For graduations and retirements, the most impactful gifts are collaborative. The gift-giver gathers photos from classmates, colleagues, teachers, family. The recipient gets dozens of perspectives on their life, not just one person's curated selection.

Fix: For milestone occasions, reach out to 10 to 15 people and ask for photos and short messages. Compile them into one book. That becomes an heirloom, not a nice gift.

Generic templates look fine on a computer screen but can disappoint in print. Photos might be too small, captions cut off, or layouts feel crowded.

The #1 Mistake People Make With Travel Photo Books

The most common problem with a travel photo book isn't bad photos, it's too many similar ones. Five near-identical shots of the same view, or a dozen almost-the-same group photos, dilute the book instead of strengthening it. A stronger travel photo book picks the single best version of each moment, then uses the extra room for variety:

For a trip covering more than one city or stop, organize chronologically by location rather than strictly by camera timestamp group all the photos from each place together, in the order you visited them, even if a few photos are slightly out of date within that stop. For very long trips, consider a two-tier structure: a divider or section break for each major location, with a tighter, curated photo set inside each one.

parts.html:
Fall lasts 12 weeks. That's it. By the time you finish putting away the summer clothes, autumn is halfway over. By November, it's gone.

This creates a unique urgency around fall photography that other seasons don't have. Spring will come again next year. Summer happens annually. But fall's particular magic (the specific golden light, your kids' current ages, the exact configuration of your family this year) only happens once. That's why fall photo books matter differently than other seasonal albums.

Most fall photo guides focus on posing and outfit coordination. Where to stand, what to wear, how to angle the light. But those guides miss the actual point. The point isn't to create a magazine-worthy portrait shoot. The point is to freeze the feeling of this particular fall with these particular people, so you can return to it in January when everything is gray and cold.

This guide covers what moments actually matter, how to organize them into a coherent story, and why the fall photo books families create now become their most-reached-for keepsakes.

Quick Summary

  • Fall is the only season with built-in urgency: 12 weeks to capture moments that never repeat exactly the same way again.
  • The best fall photo book moments aren't posed family portraits, they're the in-between moments: kids in pumpkin patches, family conversations over apple cider, transitions between seasons.
  • Most fall photos end up scattered across phones in no particular order; organizing them into a chronological book transforms them from snapshots into a story.
  • The biggest mistake is waiting until winter to start the book, by which time the feeling of fall has faded and photo selection feels like work instead of pleasure.
  • AI-powered photo organization helps handle imperfect fall photos (rain, mess, motion blur) by automatically curating and arranging them, making the album feel polished despite chaotic source material.
  • Fall family photo books consistently rank as people's most-loved keepsakes because they capture togetherness, gratitude, and seasonal beauty simultaneously.
  • There's a reason families love fall photo books. Start capturing now at Pixovo and organize as you go, so by November you have a finished keepsake.

Why Fall Deserves Its Own Photo Book (Not Just Fall Photos in a Bigger Album)

Every season has beauty. But fall is different. Fall is a season of transition, which makes it emotionally loaded in ways summer and spring aren't. Summer is about freedom. Spring is about renewal. But fall is about time passing. It's about your kids growing. It's about change arriving.

Because of this, fall photos carry weight. A photo of your child jumping in leaf piles isn't just a cute moment. It's a marker: "This is where they were this fall. This was their height, their interests, their personality at age seven." Next fall they'll be eight. The leaf pile will feel smaller to them. They might not find the same joy in jumping.

That's why a dedicated fall photo book works better than mixing fall photos into a general "family album." A fall album honors the season's specific beauty and emotional texture. It says, "This moment mattered. This season mattered. Let's remember it exactly as it was."

Also practically: fall photos often have a distinct aesthetic (golden light, warm colors, specific locations like pumpkin patches and orchards), so organizing them separately creates visual coherence. You're not jarring from summer beach photos to fall forest photos in the same book. You're building a focused story.

Fall Moments Worth Capturing (And Why)

Not every photo is worth including in a book. Some moments are fleeting but forgettable. Others are brief but essential to the story of "us in fall." Here's what actually matters:

The pattern: candid moments documenting your actual fall beat posed moments every time. A candid photo of your kid jumping in leaves, laughing, is infinitely more valuable than five posed photos of them smiling at the camera.

Common Mistakes With Fall Photo Books (And How to Avoid Them)

Mistake 1: Waiting Until November to Start the Book

By November, fall is over. The light is different. The trees are bare. And psychologically, the season has passed. Starting a fall photo book in November feels like work. Starting it in September feels like capturing something precious before it's gone.

Fix: Start the book in September. Add photos to it as you take them. By November, it's half-done already. You're not scrambling to remember what happened or digging through chaos. The album grew with the season.

Mistake 2: Only Including "Perfect" Photos

Fall photos are messy. Kids get muddy in pumpkin patches. Rain happens. Candid moments are blurry. Perfectionists wait for "good enough" photos, then end up with very few photos and a book that feels thin.

Fix: Include the imperfect photos. AI-powered tools like Pixovo automatically curate and arrange photos intelligently, so slightly blurry or imperfectly lit photos still look intentional in layout. The messiness becomes part of the story, not a liability.

Mistake 3: Treating Fall Photos as a "Photo Shoot," Not a "Season"

Most fall photo guides push you toward planned photo shoots: coordinated outfits, specific locations, dedicated time. That results in 20 beautiful posed photos and zero documentation of what fall actually felt like living through it.

Fix: Aim for a mix. Sure, do one intentional photo session if you want. But fill most of the book with candid moments from regular fall days. That's the actual story.

Mistake 4: Including Too Many Similar Photos

A pumpkin patch outing yields 50 photos. Fifty photos of similar moments: kid with pumpkin, kid with different pumpkin, kid and parent with pumpkin, repeat. In a book, three well-chosen photos from that outing tell the story better than 15 near-duplicates.

Fix: After the outing, do a hard sort. Keep the best photo from each moment (picking pumpkins, sitting in the patch, holding the final choice). Delete or archive the rest. Quality over quantity.

Fall photo books have longevity other seasonal albums don't. People return to them year after year, especially as fall approaches again.

Part of it is seasonality: fall comes once a year, so a fall book gets pulled off the shelf every September. faq.q: When is the best time to start a fall photo book?

Starting early means you're in the season while it's happening, not trying to recreate it after it's passed.

faq.q: How many fall photos should I include in a photo book?
faq.a: A good rule of thumb is one high-quality photo per book page, or 2-3 per page if you want a denser layout. For a 40-page fall album, that's 40-120 total photos. Most people have far more photos than that from a full season, so your job is curating down to the best of the shots. Quality and storytelling matter more than quantity.

faq.a: For fall photo books, 10x10 is ideal. It's large enough to showcase autumn colors and seasonal details (warm tones, textures, foliage) without being unwieldy. faq.q: Should I include Thanksgiving in the fall photo book, or make a separate Thanksgiving book?
faq.a: Either works, depending on your preference. If Thanksgiving is a central part of your fall story, spanning multiple days or locations, a dedicated Thanksgiving book might make sense. If Thanksgiving is one chapter in a larger fall album, include it in the broader book. Most people find it works best integrated into the fall album, since Thanksgiving is inherently a fall holiday.
